newsitem.title: ROMANIA: FOREIGN LAND OWNERSHIP CLEARS ROMANIA PARLIAMENT.
newsitem.headline: FOREIGN LAND OWNERSHIP CLEARS ROMANIA PARLIAMENT.

text.p: Romania's parliament's lower house on Tuesday has passed a bill on foreign land ownership, which analysts say is pivotal to attracting foreign investment.
"Deputies endorsed the draft in a matter of minutes," a press officer with parliament's lower Chamber of Deputies said.

The law, which previously cleared the upper Senate and is awaiting presidential approval, gives Romania-based companies with fully or partly foreign capital "the right of property and any other real rights over the land they need to carry out their activity during their existence."
It virtually amends a 1991 foreign investment law which gave foreigners land ownership rights only through local companies having at least one Romanian shareholder.
Existing Romanian legislation does not forbid foreign ownership of buildings.
Analysts and foreign investors welcome the new law saying it was crushing one of the main stumbling blocks to foreign investment, helping to boost direct capital inflows.

"This is a positive step towards removing barriers to foreign investment," a foreign investor with an operation in Romania told Reuters. "Land ownership is something investors are looking at when considering potential capital inputs."

The reformist government, which replaced former leftists after elections last November, has pledged to remove obstacles to foreign investors and stimulate capital inflows by boosting facilities, including tax cuts, and fighting red tape.
It also said it would encourage foreign investment through privatisation, by putting on sale stakes in attractive companies, including public utilities.
"Romania's new move will make it a lot more attractive, helping foreign investment pick up," another investor said.

Direct foreign investment in Romania is a lot lower than elsewhere in the region. In seven years since it shed communism, Romania -- Eastern Europe's second largest market after Poland -- has attracted a little over $2.0 billion.
Bureaucracy and corruption, inadequate corporate laws and tax and accounting rules, as well as slow privatisation have often been cited as the main hindrances to foreign investment.
